rv.q: Snow in Midsummer is a wonderful engagement with classical Chinese literature and folkloric storytelling through modern sensibilities.
The concept is strong, and Snow in Midsummer is worth supporting as, hopefully, one of many future Eastern dramas on major New York stages.
As a result, you’ll probably never bored, though you might be confused – even when you exit the theater.
The venerable tale might have been updated in any old way.
Too melodramatic and unconvincing to succeed, Snow in Midsummer exerts the lurid interest of a crime scene, but real engagement is undermined by ponderous pacing and an unearned air of solemnity.

Which is to say that the play is something of a soap opera. But thanks to some impassioned performances, sharp direction by Zi Alikhan , and a script that leans heavily into ancient Chinese beliefs regarding death and the afterlife, the production is never less than gripping.

cn.t: Cowhig's ambitious adaptation of a 13th-century Chinese tale draws mixed reactions. Critics appreciate its exploration of injustice and patriarchy, but find the plot twists and tonal shifts uneven in this modern murder mystery framework.
